step1_summary: Chief complaint: Sudden‐onset shortness of breath with right-sided pleuritic back pain.

Current symptoms: • Began today – sharp pain on deep inspiration in right back, breathlessness. • Coughed up small amounts of blood twice. • Subjective ‘slight fever’. • Awareness of heartbeat/palpitations. • Two-week history of tiredness, reduced exercise tolerance, daily activities harder.
Aggravating/alleviating factors: Pain worsens with deep breath; no stated relieving factors.
Past medical history: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
Family history: No known venous thrombo-embolism or bleeding disorders.
Social history: 45-year-old woman; non-smoker; office desk job; lives alone in a flat; owns a cat; no recent long-haul flights.

Vital signs / exam (video): • Radial pulse counted at 66–74 bpm, regular. • Capillary refill normal. • Oropharynx unremarkable. • No cervical lymphadenopathy. • Appears clinically stable on video. • Temperature, BP, RR, SpO₂ not measured.

V: Pulmonary embolism with pulmonary infarction: acute pleuritic pain, SOB and minor haemoptysis; SLE confers hypercoagulable risk.
I: Community-acquired pneumonia (incl. lobar pneumonia): fever, pleuritic pain, cough ± haemoptysis, acute onset, immunosuppressed host.
Tuberculosis: haemoptysis and constitutional symptoms possible, but onset usually subacute/chronic.
N: Primary lung carcinoma or bronchial carcinoid: haemoptysis and fatigue; less likely given abrupt onset and non-smoker.
D: Methotrexate-related interstitial lung disease: drug can cause acute pneumonitis with cough and dyspnoea.
I2: Drug-induced alveolar haemorrhage (methotrexate): would explain haemoptysis and dyspnoea.
C: Pulmonary arteriovenous malformation: congenital cause of unexplained haemoptysis.
A: SLE-related pleuritis or diffuse alveolar haemorrhage: lupus flare can produce pleuritic pain and haemoptysis.
T: Minor thoracic musculoskeletal strain with coincidental upper-airway bleed (less likely—no trauma).
E: Anemia secondary to chronic disease causing fatigue (does not explain haemoptysis).

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Most common cause of acute pleuritic chest pain with fever, cough and haemoptysis, especially in an immunosuppressed patient on methotrexate.
Classic triad of pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea and haemoptysis; SLE increases clot risk, though pulse normal and no obvious provoking factors.
Patient is actively taking methotrexate; drug can cause acute interstitial pneumonitis and haemoptysis, but it is uncommon and usually subacute.
Underlying SLE could flare with pleuritic pain or diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, yet no other flare signs reported.
Haemoptysis and fatigue fit, but presentation is typically insidious; patient is a non-smoker with very acute onset of symptoms.

supporting_evidence: Acute onset fever and pleuritic chest/back pain
Immunosuppression from methotrexate increases infection risk
opposing_evidence: No documented tachycardia, tachypnoea or abnormal lung sounds (not yet auscultated)
Cough described only for one day
Normal heart rate (66–74 bpm) rather than tachycardia
No leg pain/swelling, recent surgery or travel
Symptoms started very suddenly only today (PE possible but less common without risk factors)

supporting_evidence: On methotrexate, took dose this morning
Can present with acute cough, dyspnoea and sometimes haemoptysis
opposing_evidence: Haemoptysis uncommon; more often dry cough
Usually subacute over days–weeks, not sudden same-day onset
Fever less typical unless secondary infection

supporting_evidence: Pleuritic chest pain and haemoptysis compatible with lupus pulmonary involvement
opposing_evidence: No other lupus flare symptoms (joint pain, rash, serositis elsewhere)
Very acute onset limited to one day

supporting_evidence: Fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance for 2 weeks
opposing_evidence: Extremely acute onset of pain and fever argues for infective/inflammatory rather than neoplastic cause
No chronic cough or weight loss reported
